briefs.text: Afghanistan is among the world's poorest economies, with GDP per capita of $417 in 2024. The World Bank estimates the economy contracted by about 25% after August 2021, amid sharp declines in international aid. Prices fell 6.6% in 2024, and the trade deficit ($9.3 bn) was about half of GDP; there is no recent Comtrade report.

Albania's growth is tourism-led, according to the IMF, which notes that tourism continues to provide steady support to output. GDP was $30.5 bn in 2025, or about $13,000 per person, with unemployment at 10.9%. Goods imports ($9.6 bn in 2024) were more than twice goods exports ($4.0 bn), which lean on footwear and clothing and go mainly to Italy (44%). Personal remittances equalled about 8.4% of GDP in 2025 (World Bank).

Algeria is a hydrocarbon exporter: petroleum gases (47.9%), crude oil (27.4%) and refined oil (16.1%) made up over 90% of its $51.9 bn goods exports in 2024, sold mainly to Italy, France and Spain. It was the world's 10th-largest natural gas producer in 2024 and ranked 5th among reporters for gas exports. It is also a major food importer, ranking 3rd among reporters for wheat imports ($3.0 bn, 2024). GDP was $287 bn in 2025 and unemployment 11.6%.

American Samoa, a US territory, is unusual in the Pacific for its export-oriented tuna canning industry, which US trade policy helped establish; a fall in exports of canned tuna drove the decline in real GDP in 2021. Government is the dominant employer, paying 64% of total compensation in 2021. GDP was $871 m in 2022, about $18,000 per head; newer GDP and trade data are not available.

Andorra is a euroized microstate that the IMF describes as dependent on a few sectors (tourism, banking and construction) and tightly linked to Spain and France. With about 83,000 residents and GDP per person of $54,292 in 2025, it ran a current-account surplus the IMF estimates at 15.9% of GDP in 2025. The IMF also notes that its banks' assets under management reached 21 times GDP in 2023. Spain took 53% of its small goods exports ($221 m) in 2025.

Angola is an oil economy: crude oil made up 72.5% of its $33.7 bn goods exports in 2025, with petroleum gas adding 9.6% and diamonds 5.3%. China took 43% of those exports. The economy was worth $122 bn in 2025 (about $3,100 per person), and inflation stayed high at 20.2%.

Anguilla, a UK territory that uses the East Caribbean dollar, depends heavily on tourism, which accounts for 37% of GDP according to the IMF (2024). Sales of '.ai' internet domain names have become a major new source of public revenue: in 2023 they brought in EC$87 m (about US$32 m), just over 20% of government revenue. The project's datasets hold no GDP or recent goods-trade figures for the territory.

Antarctica has no permanent economy; under the Antarctic Treaty system it is a natural reserve devoted to peace and science, and mineral resource activities other than scientific research are prohibited.

Antigua and Barbuda is a tourism economy: the IMF credits tourism for 4.3% growth in 2024, when output passed pre-pandemic levels, and for helping cut public debt from about 100% of GDP in 2020 to 67% in 2024. GDP per head was $24,800 in 2025, and net FDI inflows equalled 12% of GDP. Goods trade is lopsided, with $33 m of exports against $663 m of imports in 2024, more than half of them from the US.

Argentina is a major farm exporter with a history of very high inflation: consumer prices rose 220% in 2024. Maize, soybean oil and soybean meal each made up 6-7% of its $87 bn goods exports in 2025, though 30% of exports are recorded as unspecified commodities. It produced 12% of the world's soybeans in 2024 and holds 13% of world lithium reserves, the third-largest. Brazil and China are its main trade partners, and government debt was 80% of GDP in 2025.

Armenia is a small, fast-growing economy (GDP $29.2 bn, growth 7.2% in 2025) whose goods trade runs heavily through Russia and the UAE, which took 35% and 25% of its $8.3 bn exports in 2025. Gold (16%), jewellery (13%), smartphones (11%) and copper ore (8%) led exports, while gold and phones were also the top imports. Unemployment was high at 12.9% in 2025.

Aruba, part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, is a tourism economy: the IMF attributes its rapid growth in 2023–24 to private hotel investment and strong tourism, and the World Bank puts 2024 growth at 6.8%. GDP per head was $38,600 in 2024 and unemployment 4.0% in 2025, with government debt at 65% of GDP. Goods exports are small ($111 m in 2023), and over half were cigars and cigarettes, with Colombia taking 46%.

Australia was the leading exporter of both iron ore and coal among reporting countries in 2025: iron ore made up 23% of its $336 bn goods exports in 2025 and coal 12%, with LNG and gold close behind, and China took 30%. It also led world lithium output in 2024 (37%) and holds large reserves of nickel, cobalt, copper and manganese. With GDP of $1.8 tn and income of $65,000 per head (2025), it is a rich economy whose exports are highly resource-based.

Austria is a rich, diversified economy ($62,930 GDP per capita in 2025) tightly bound to Germany, which took 29.6% of its goods exports and supplied 31.4% of its imports in 2025. Its $213.6 bn of goods exports are widely spread, led by blood and biological products (5.1%), cars (4.1%) and medicines (3.5%). Growth was weak at 0.6% in 2025, and net FDI inflows were negative (-$11.7 bn), signalling disinvestment.

Azerbaijan is a hydrocarbon exporter: crude oil (48%) and natural gas (35%) made up about 84% of its $25.0 bn goods exports in 2025, with Italy alone taking 45% and Türkiye 14%. Growth was a modest 1.4% in 2025 and government debt a low 20% of GDP. Gold was the largest import, at 26% of the total.

The Bahamas lives on tourism and international finance: IMF staff expected 2025 growth of 2.8% to come mainly from construction and cruise tourism, and the IMF put the international financial sector at about 21 times GDP in 2018. GDP per head was $39,500 in 2024, and government debt stood at 72% of GDP in 2025. Goods exports ($944 m in 2024, led by refined petroleum) are small next to $4.9 bn of imports, 86% of them from the US.

Bahrain stands out among Gulf economies for its government debt, which the IMF puts at 144% of GDP in 2025. Its reported goods exports ($12.5 bn in 2024) are led by aluminium in various forms (about 36%) and iron ore (14%), with Saudi Arabia (23%) and the UAE (14%) as main buyers; iron ore and alumina are also its top imports. GDP per capita was $30,600 in 2025.

Bangladesh, with 176 million people and a $456 bn economy in 2025, is built on garment exports: knitwear and woven garments together supplied about 82% of export earnings in July-September 2024, according to Bangladesh Bank. It is also the third-largest rice producer (7.4% of world output in 2024). Inflation was 8.8% and growth slowed to 3.5% in 2025. No Comtrade report has been filed in the last three years.

Barbados is a services economy driven by tourism, business services and construction, which IMF staff credited for about 4% growth in 2024. Government debt remains high at 96% of GDP in 2025; the island completed IMF-supported programmes backing its home-grown BERT recovery plan in June 2025. GDP per head was $28,400 in 2025. Goods exports of $421 m in 2025 were led by refined petroleum (29%) and spirits (11%), against imports of $2.3 bn.

Since 2022 Belarus has become far more dependent on Russia. BEROC economist Dzmitry Kruk (2024) estimates that Russia takes around 60-65% of Belarus's exports, up from about 35-40% before 2022, and the Centre for Eastern Studies (OSW, 2023) notes that fuel and potash exports now rely on transit through Russian ports and railways. Belarus has filed no Comtrade report in the last three years, so these shares come from those studies. GDP was $93.4 bn in 2025 ($10,279 per person), with growth of 1.3%, inflation of 6.6% and government debt at 31% of GDP.

Belgium is a very open economy: its goods exports of $382.7 bn in 2025 were equal to over half of its $725.5 bn GDP, led by medicines (7.6%), blood and biological products (7.5%), cars and refined petroleum. Germany, France and the Netherlands together took over 40% of exports, and the Netherlands supplied 22.9% of imports. Government debt is high at 107.9% of GDP (2025), and net FDI inflows were negative (-$28.8 bn), indicating disinvestment.

Belize is a small open economy of 423,000 people (2025) that depends heavily on tourism, which contributes directly about 12% of GDP according to the national Tourism Satellite Account cited by the IMF. Its goods exports are modest ($242 m in 2025) and agricultural, led by sugar (24%) and bananas (19%) and sold mainly to the UK and the US, while imports were about six times larger at $1.5 bn. Government debt was 67% of GDP in 2025.

Benin's official trade data reveal little: 99% of its reported 2025 goods exports were 'commodities not specified', which is not a product category. The IMF describes an export model that relies on transit and re-export trade through the Port of Cotonou, mostly to Nigeria, and on cotton, its traditional export. GDP grew 8.1% in 2025 to $24.6 bn ($1,658 per person), with inflation of 1.1%.

Bermuda, a British overseas territory, is one of the richest places in the world per person, with GDP per capita of about $142,000 in 2024. Its economy rests on international business, chiefly insurance and reinsurance: the government reports this sector as the largest contributor to real GDP in 2024 and, with tourism, the main source of foreign exchange. Goods trade is small: exports were $42 m in 2025 (mostly aircraft and vessels), against $1.2 bn of imports, 78% from the US.

Bhutan's exports have rested on hydropower sold to India: the ADB reports that electricity, all of it exported to India, made up 68% of total exports in FY2023, though a later ADB report puts hydropower at about 30% of exports in FY2024. UN Comtrade's reported goods exports for 2025 ($519 m) are led by ferro-alloys (43%), with India taking 78%, and do not show electricity among the top products. Government debt is high at 103% of GDP (2025).

Bolivia's economy is under strain: GDP contracted 1.6% in 2025, inflation reached 19.5% and government debt was 83% of GDP. The IMF's 2025 review links this to rapidly falling natural gas output and large central-bank-financed deficits under a fixed exchange rate, which have nearly exhausted usable foreign-exchange reserves. Its $9.7 bn of goods exports in 2025 are mineral-heavy, led by precious-metal ores (18%), zinc ores (15%), gold (12%) and natural gas (11%), and go mainly to China, Brazil and India. Refined fuel made up 30% of goods imports.

Bosnia and Herzegovina runs a large trade gap: goods imports of $17.3 bn in 2025 were almost twice exports of $9.8 bn. Its exports are unusually diversified, with electricity the largest item at only 5.1%, and they go mostly to neighbours and the EU (Croatia 18%, Germany 14%, Serbia 12%). The convertible mark operates under a currency board arrangement, and remittances equalled about 10.7% of GDP in 2025. GDP was $32.6 bn, or $10,382 per person.

Botswana is a diamond economy: diamonds made up 63.9% of its $3.9 bn goods exports in 2024, with copper ore adding 18.8%. Income is relatively high at about $7,800 per person in 2025, but GDP shrank 0.7% that year, net FDI inflows were negative (-$649 m, a disinvestment), and unemployment was 24.5%.

Brazil, a $2.3 tn economy of 213 m people (2025), is a leading exporter of farm and mineral commodities. It grew 36% of the world's soybeans in 2024, was the top reporter of soybean exports ($43.5 bn) in 2025 and is the second-largest iron ore producer. Crude oil (13%), soybeans (12.5%) and iron ore (8%) led its $349 bn of goods exports, with China taking 29%. It also holds large graphite, rare-earth and nickel reserves. Government debt was 93% of GDP in 2025.

The British Indian Ocean Territory is home to the military base on Diego Garcia. In October 2024 the UK and Mauritius announced a political agreement under which Mauritius would hold sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago while the UK would be authorised to keep operating the base for an initial 99 years. The project's datasets hold no economic figures for it.

The British Virgin Islands, a UK territory of about 40,000 people, record enormous cross-border investment flows for their size: net FDI inflows of $42.9 bn and outflows of $47.2 bn in 2025, reflecting their role as one of the Caribbean offshore financial centres reviewed by the IMF. The territory's 2026 budget names financial services and tourism as the main economic drivers. The project's datasets hold no GDP or recent goods-trade figures for it.

Brunei is a small hydrocarbon economy: in 2025 refined fuels, natural gas, crude oil and cyclic hydrocarbons together made up about 91% of its $10.3 billion goods exports, sold mainly to Australia, China and Japan. Crude oil was also 61% of its imports, with Malaysia the largest supplier of goods overall (35%). GDP per capita was about $32,000 in 2025 ($92,000 at PPP), government debt only 1.6% of GDP, and growth 0.7%.

Bulgaria became the 21st member of the euro area on 1 January 2026. Its government debt is low, at 29.9% of GDP in 2025. Exports are broad-based, with refined copper the largest identified product at 4.4% of $47.9 bn in goods exports; copper ore is also a significant import. Germany (14%) and Romania (11%) are the main markets. GDP was $131 bn in 2025, or $20,328 per person, with unemployment at 3.5%.

Burkina Faso is a gold economy: gold made up 82.3% of its $5.6 bn goods exports in 2024, shipped mainly to Switzerland (56.2%) and the UAE (26.2%), with cotton a distant second at 5.9%. Refined fuel accounted for 36.6% of imports. GDP was $27.6 bn in 2025 ($1,148 per person), growth 5.3%, and consumer prices fell 0.6%.

Burundi's income of about $234 per person in 2025 was the lowest in Eastern Africa, and consumer prices rose 34.1% that year. Its goods exports were only $170 m in 2023, led by coffee (24.8%), gold (18.0%) and tea (10.8%). The DR Congo and the UAE were its main buyers. Imports, a fifth of them fuel, were about seven times larger at $1.2 bn.

Cabo Verde is a small island economy built on tourism, which the World Bank says contributes about 25% of GDP directly and up to 44% including indirect effects. Goods exports were just $81 m in 2025, 87% of it prepared fish sent mainly to Spain, against $1.1 bn of imports, almost half from Portugal. Government debt was high at 115.4% of GDP in 2025, while GDP per capita was $5,796 and growth 6.3%.

Cambodia is a labour-intensive export manufacturer: knitwear, clothing and travel goods lead its diversified $31.3 billion of goods exports in 2025, with the US taking 41%, while China supplied 53% of imports. Research shows the garment industry has led its industrialisation, and that it became one of Asia's most dollarised economies, fed by dollar inflows from garments, tourism, FDI and aid. FDI inflows equalled about 10% of GDP in 2025, and GDP per capita was about $2,900.

Cameroon's exports are spread more widely than those of most Central African producers. In 2023 crude oil (37.7%) and petroleum gas (14.1%) led goods exports, followed by cocoa beans (12.0%), sawn wood (6.7%) and cotton (4.9%). At $58.9 bn in 2025, it is the largest economy in the CFA franc zone of Central Africa, with moderate inflation (3.4%) and government debt (40.5% of GDP).

Canada is a $2.3 tn economy (2025) and one of the world's major commodity exporters. Crude oil made up 18% of its $556 bn goods exports in 2025; it was the fourth-largest crude oil producer in 2024 and the top reporter of wheat exports in 2025, and it is also a leading producer of nickel, cobalt and palladium. Trade is tied to the US, which took 72% of goods exports in 2025. General government debt was 114% of GDP in 2025.

The Cayman Islands, a UK territory, had GDP per head of $104,000 in 2024, built on financial services, which account for over 30% of GDP according to the territory's statistics office. Its role as an offshore financial centre shows in large and volatile investment flows: net FDI inflows were $35.8 bn in 2025, against GDP of $7.8 bn in 2024. Goods trade is small and one-sided, with $56 m of exports against $1.7 bn of imports in 2024, 82% of them from the US.

The Central African Republic has one of the world's lowest incomes, with GDP of $3.1 bn and about $556 per person in 2025. Its recorded goods exports were only $205 m in 2024, and half of that value was classified under aircraft and parts (HS8807), so the records say little about domestic production; gold (15.7%) and diamonds (6.3%) were the main resource exports. Refined fuel was the largest import (26.3%), and Cameroon (26.4%) and China (24.6%) were the main suppliers.

Chad's economy rests on oil: the World Bank reports that in 2024 the oil sector made up 14.3% of GDP, 51.8% of fiscal revenues and 65.3% of exports. GDP grew 5.6% in 2025 to $21.5 bn, or about $1,000 per person, and consumer prices fell 3.9%. Chad has filed no UN Comtrade report in the last three years, so detailed goods-trade data are missing.

Chile is the world's largest copper producer, with 23% of global mine output in 2024, and copper ores and refined copper made up about half of its $110 bn goods exports in 2025. It also holds the largest lithium reserves (31% of the world total) and was the top reporter of lithium exports. China bought 37% of its goods exports. Government debt was moderate at 42% of GDP in 2025, while unemployment was 9.0%.

China, a $19.5 trillion economy in 2025, dominates the supply of many industrial raw materials: in 2024 it mined about 69% of the world's rare earths, 79% of natural graphite and 83% of tungsten, refined 99% of gallium, and produced over half of the world's coal. Its $3.78 trillion of goods exports in 2025 were highly diversified, led by smartphones, chips and computers, with the US taking 11%. It was the largest importer of crude oil, iron ore and soybeans among reporting countries in 2025, and its surplus on goods and services trade reached $816 billion.

Colombia's $50 bn of goods exports in 2025 were led by commodities: crude oil (20%), coffee (12%), gold (9%) and coal (8%), with cut flowers another 5%. The US took 30% of exports, while China was the largest source of imports. A $457 bn economy of 53 m people (2025), it ran a goods-and-services trade deficit of $24.7 bn, and government debt was 60% of GDP.

The Comoros depends heavily on money sent home by its diaspora: a 2024 study describes it as Africa's second-largest recipient of remittances relative to GDP. Its goods exports are tiny ($31 m in 2025) and dominated by cloves (78.7%) plus essential oils and vanilla, with India buying 55.5%. Imports, led by rice and cement, were ten times larger at $312 m.

The Cook Islands, listed in the project's data under New Zealand and using the New Zealand dollar, depends heavily on tourism, its largest economic driver; researchers describe it as close to a tourism mono-economy, exposed when borders closed during COVID-19. The project's datasets hold no recent GDP or trade figures for it.

Costa Rica has become a high-tech manufacturing exporter: medical instruments made up 34% of its $19.9 bn goods exports in 2024 and orthopaedic appliances another 8%, ahead of fresh fruit and bananas. The IMF and OECD credit free trade zones and foreign investment, and the OECD notes that medical devices and business services now exceed agricultural commodities and tourism as top exports. GDP grew 4.6% in 2025, FDI inflows equalled 5.4% of GDP, and the US took 48% of goods exports in 2024.

Côte d'Ivoire's $29.4 bn goods exports in 2025 rest on several commodities: cocoa beans (23.9%), gold (16.0%), natural rubber (11.8%), cashew nuts (7.4%) and crude oil (6.1%), with Switzerland and the Netherlands the top destinations. It ran a $5.0 bn surplus on goods and services in 2025, while GDP grew 6.5% to $99.8 bn, about $3,050 per person, with inflation of just 0.1%.

Tourism is Croatia's signature industry: it generated 12.2% of GDP directly in 2022 and about 66% of service exports in 2024, according to the OECD. Croatia joined the euro area in January 2023. GDP reached $105 bn in 2025, or $27,104 per person, with unemployment at 5.0%. Goods trade is diverse and regional: refined petroleum was the top export at only 6.1%, and goods imports ($50.1 bn) were much larger than exports ($28.2 bn).

Cuba is going through its most severe economic crisis since at least the collapse of the Soviet Union, according to a 2025 economic report by the Swiss embassy in Havana; GDP fell 1.1% in 2024. Official data are sparse: the latest World Bank nominal GDP figure is $107 bn for 2020, and no Comtrade goods trade has been reported in the last three years. The island holds 500,000 t of cobalt reserves (2024), 4.5% of the world total and the fourth largest.

Curaçao, part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, has pivoted to a tourism-led economy after the decline of its offshore financial sector and its oil refining industry, according to the IMF (2025). GDP was $3.6 bn in 2024 ($22,800 per head) and grew 5.0%. No Comtrade goods trade has been reported in the last three years.

Cyprus, a euro-area island economy with GDP per capita of $41,800 in 2025, recorded FDI inflows of $11.2 bn that year, equal to 27% of GDP; the IMF notes it hosts numerous special purpose entities, mainly in finance and shipping, that distort its macroeconomic and external statistics. Its $6.3 bn goods exports in 2025 were dominated by refined petroleum (49%), a quarter of all exports going to Libya, followed by ships (12%), medicines (8%) and cheese (7%).

Czechia is a car- and electronics-assembly economy closely tied to Germany, which took 31.5% of its $282 bn of goods exports in 2025. Cars (13.7%), computers (6.6%), car parts (6.3%) and phones (5.5%) lead its exports, and it ran a goods-and-services surplus of $22.9 bn. GDP was $391 bn in 2025, or $35,917 per person. Unemployment was very low at 2.8%, and government debt was moderate at 44% of GDP.

The DR Congo is the world's dominant cobalt supplier, mining 76% of global output in 2024 and holding 55% of reserves. It is also the second-largest copper producer. Refined copper alone made up 63.6% of its $37.4 bn goods exports in 2024, and China bought 58.9%. With 113 m people, income was still only about $810 per person in 2025.

Denmark's exports are anchored in pharmaceuticals: medicines made up 13.0% of its $148.5 bn of goods exports in 2025, with hormones and blood products also prominent, alongside pork. The economy is rich ($76,970 GDP per capita) and grew 2.9% in 2025, combining low government debt (27.4% of GDP) with a $50.9 bn trade surplus and large outward FDI (11.4% of GDP). About a fifth of goods exports (19.8%) are reported without a named destination, under Comtrade's 'Special Categories' partner code.

Djibouti is a port and logistics economy serving landlocked Ethiopia. The IMF reports that re-exports, mainly to Ethiopia, make up over 90% of its goods exports. This is why Comtrade shows Ethiopia taking 83.5% of exports in 2023, led by palm oil, other vegetable oils, sugar and vehicles. Growth was 6.5% in 2025, but unemployment stood at 26.0%.

Dominica carries public debt of about 100% of GDP (99.9% in 2025), and the IMF calls citizenship-by-investment (CBI) inflows an essential source of development financing while urging less reliance on them. Growth of 3.5% in 2024 came from a tourism recovery, increasingly driven by cruise passengers. Goods exports are tiny ($22 m in 2023), led by machinery parts and bananas, against $301 m of imports.

The Dominican Republic has achieved the fastest income convergence in Latin America and the Caribbean over the past two decades, according to the IMF, reaching GDP of $127 bn in 2025 ($11,100 per head). Comtrade shows a diversified 2025 goods basket led by gold (17%), medical instruments (13%) and cigars and cigarettes (7%), with the US taking 54%. The IMF says exports and remittances support the current account, whose deficit is fully financed by FDI; net FDI inflows were $4.9 bn in 2025.

Ecuador has officially adopted the US dollar as its currency (IMF) and exports mainly food and oil: shrimp and other crustaceans made up 23% of its $37 bn goods exports in 2025, ahead of crude oil (19%), bananas (12%) and cocoa beans (11%). Its buyers are split between the US, Panama and China. Inflation was just 0.7% in 2025, the economy ran a $4.6 bn trade surplus, and government debt was 55% of GDP.

Egypt, with 118 m people and $365 bn GDP in 2025, imported about twice as many goods as it exported ($101 bn against $51 bn in 2025) and was the largest wheat importer among reporters. The IMF names remittances, tourism receipts, petroleum exports and Suez Canal revenue as the main offsets to its widening hydrocarbon trade deficit. Inflation was 14.1% and government debt 86.8% of GDP in 2025, while FDI inflows reached $15.5 bn.

El Salvador has used the US dollar as legal tender since 2001 (IMF) and leans heavily on money sent home by migrants: a Federal Reserve note reports remittances above 20% of GDP in 2023. Its $6.4 bn of goods exports in 2025 are diversified, led by knitted apparel such as T-shirts and jerseys, and go mainly to the US (33%) and Central American neighbours. Imports were nearly three times exports at $17.8 bn, and government debt was 88% of GDP in 2025.

Equatorial Guinea is a hydrocarbon economy with shrinking oil output. According to the World Bank, hydrocarbons made up about 46% of GDP and over 80% of government revenue in 2024, and crude oil production fell 6.8% that year. Output fell 5.8% in 2025, though GDP per person was still $6,615. There has been no Comtrade report in the last three years.

Eritrea is one of the least documented economies. The latest IMF macro figures date from 2019, when GDP was about $2.0 bn and government debt 260% of GDP, and there has been no Comtrade report in the last three years. The World Bank says zinc, copper and gold account for over 90% of exports, put public debt at around 219% of GDP at end-2023, and notes that about 70% of people live in rural areas relying on rain-fed farming, livestock and fishing.

Estonia is a small, open economy of 1.4 m people with widely spread exports: its $21.5 bn of goods exports in 2025 included phones, cars, refined fuels and wooden joinery, with Finland (14.7%) and its Baltic neighbours as leading markets. Income reached $52,106 per head at PPP in 2025 and public debt is low (24.0% of GDP), but growth was 0.6%, inflation 4.8% and unemployment 8.3%, while net FDI inflows turned negative (-$1.0 bn).

Eswatini is closely tied to South Africa, which took 67.5% of its exports and supplied 73.8% of its imports in 2023. Its largest export lines that year were odoriferous mixtures (27.9%) and sugar (18.8%); the IMF names sugar and soft-drink concentrates as key export drivers. According to the IMF, Southern African Customs Union transfers averaged 39% of government revenue over the past five years. Unemployment was very high at 34.2% in 2025.

Ethiopia, with 135.5 m people, grew a rapid 9.8% in 2025 to a $126.4 bn economy. Income was still only about $930 per person. Goods exports were small, at $2.9 bn in 2023, led by coffee (42.9%), oilseeds, pulses and cut flowers. Imports were nearly six times larger at $17.1 bn, a third of them from China. FDI inflows reached $3.8 bn in 2025.

The Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory, has no figures in the project's datasets. The Falkland Islands Government's national accounts show fishing, notably for squid, as by far the largest activity, at about 58% of nominal GDP in 2024, when GDP was about £288 m; its share has swung between 38% and 63% since 2014.

The Faroe Islands, a dependency of Denmark with 54,900 people, live on fish: fresh, frozen, filleted and dried fish made up about 85% of their $2.1 bn of goods exports in 2025, with the USA, Denmark, Spain and the UK the largest markets. The export base is therefore highly concentrated. GDP per capita was $74,175 in 2024, and imports, led by refined fuel (12.5%) and animal feed, come chiefly from Denmark (21.0%) and Norway (18.8%).

Fiji's economy, with GDP of $6.2 bn in 2025, relies heavily on tourism, which the IMF credits with driving its post-pandemic recovery. Its goods trade is small and in deficit: exports of $1.1 bn in 2025 were led by fuel, bottled water and gold, against imports of $3.2 bn. Government debt was 77% of GDP in 2025, and consumer prices fell 1.4%.

Finland's exports still reflect its forests: paper and paperboard (4.1%), chemical wood pulp (3.3%) and sawn wood (3.1%) were among the top goods exports in 2025, alongside refined petroleum (6.9%), out of a $84.1 bn total, with Sweden, the USA and Germany the leading markets. The economy is rich ($56,149 GDP per capita) but stagnated in 2025, growing 0.2%, with unemployment at 9.5% and government debt at 88.4% of GDP.

France is a large, diversified economy ($3.37 tn GDP in 2025) whose leading goods exports are aircraft (5.1% of $689.2 bn in 2025), medicines and jet engines. It is also a farm power: the 8th-largest wheat producer in 2024 (3.3% of world output) and the 5th-largest wheat and maize exporter among Comtrade reporters in 2025. Growth was 0.8% in 2025, the economy ran a $13.7 bn trade deficit, and government debt reached 115.5% of GDP.

French Polynesia, a French territory with GDP of $6.3 bn in 2024 (about $22,400 per head), lives mainly on tourism, followed by cultured black pearls, its second-largest income source. Pearls made up 33% of recorded goods exports in 2025, which totalled just $233 m against $2.3 bn of imports; 58% of exports were not specified by product. A 1999 study described an economy long supported by French public transfers. Unemployment was 11.7% in 2025.

The French Southern and Antarctic Lands' main economic activity is fishing in their waters: the companies catching Patagonian toothfish and lobster there had turnover of €129 m in 2017, according to INSEE. The project's datasets hold no other economic figures for them.

Gabon combines oil with manganese. In 2023 crude oil made up 51.8% of goods exports and manganese ore 23.3%, and in 2024 Gabon mined 23% of the world's manganese, second only to South Africa. Its income of about $8,260 per person in 2025 is well above most of its Central African neighbours'. But government debt was high at 84.2% of GDP, and unemployment stood at 20.2%.

Georgia has become a regional car-trading hub: motor cars were 38.6% of its $7.3 bn exports in 2025, and re-exports made up about 54% of all exports, with Kyrgyzstan (21%) and Kazakhstan (13%) the top destinations. Cars were also the largest import (21%). Growth reached 7.5% in 2025, but unemployment stayed high at 12.1% and the trade deficit was $2.2 bn.

Germany's $5.05 tn economy (2025) is built on manufactured exports: goods exports of $1.77 tn in 2025 were led by cars (10.0%), medicines and car parts, and the economy ran a $119 bn surplus on goods and services. The USA was its largest export market (9.4%), while China supplied 12.9% of imports. It is also a large raw-material importer, ranking 3rd among reporters for natural gas imports ($32.1 bn). Growth was only 0.2% in 2025, though unemployment stayed low at 3.7%.

Ghana's exports are dominated by gold, 63.1% of its $32.0 bn goods exports in 2025, sold mostly to the UAE, India, Switzerland and South Africa; cocoa beans and paste (11.4%) and crude oil (8.3%) follow. It was also the world's 4th-largest manganese producer in 2024 (4.1% of output). GDP was $114 bn in 2025 with growth of 6.0%, though inflation remained elevated at 14.2%.

Greece carries very high public debt, at 146.6% of GDP in 2025. The IMF notes large net services exports, mainly from tourism and shipping, which partly offset a large goods deficit: goods imports of $90 bn against exports of $54 bn in 2025. Refined petroleum made up 22% of goods exports, reflecting refineries that, the IMF notes, import crude and ship refined products to the rest of Europe. GDP was $281 bn in 2025 and unemployment 8.5%.

Greenland, a self-governing territory of Denmark with about 57,000 people (2025), had GDP of $3.3 bn in 2023. Danmarks Nationalbank describes goods exports as almost entirely seafood, with shrimp the most important species, and noted in 2019 that the Danish block grant supplied just over half of the Greenlandic government's revenue. There is no recent Comtrade report for Greenland.

Grenada grew an estimated 4.4% in 2025, led by investment and construction; the IMF names dependence on tourism and imports and exposure to natural disasters as key risks, and credits prudent saving of citizenship-by-investment revenue for fiscal room. Government debt was 69% of GDP and net FDI inflows 12% of GDP in 2025. Goods exports ($43 m in 2024) include wheat flour, animal feed and nutmeg (8%).

Guam, a US territory, has an unusually large government sector: it made up 40% of GDP in 2021, against 12% for the rest of the United States, according to US statistics. GDP was $6.9 bn in 2022, about $41,800 per head, and grew 5.1% that year as visitor arrivals returned. More recent GDP figures and goods trade data are not available.

Guatemala, with GDP of $123 bn and 18.7 m people in 2025, relies heavily on remittances, which the IMF says reached a record 21% of GDP in 2025. Its $15.6 bn of goods exports are diversified, led by coffee, bananas, sugar and palm oil, and go mainly to the US, El Salvador and Honduras. Goods imports were more than twice exports, while government debt was low at 27% of GDP in 2025.

Guernsey, a dependency of the United Kingdom that uses the pound sterling, has no World Bank, IMF or Comtrade figures in this dataset. Its own statistics office estimates GDP at £3.49 bn in 2023, with financial and insurance activities the largest sector at about 37% of GDP.

Guinea holds the world's largest bauxite reserves (25.5% of the global total) and was the top producer in 2024, mining 130 million tonnes, 28.9% of world output. FDI inflows reached $7.8 bn in 2025, an exceptional 27.4% of GDP. GDP grew 7.4% to $28.3 bn ($1,877 per person). Guinea has filed no Comtrade report in the last three years, so its export mix is not shown here.

Guinea-Bissau is a mono-crop economy: the World Bank puts cashew nuts at around 90% of export value, and a strong 2025 cashew harvest drove growth of 5.8% that year. GDP was $2.5 bn in 2025 ($1,124 per person) and government debt 75.1% of GDP. The country has filed no Comtrade report in the last three years.

Guyana's economy has been transformed by oil: since production began at end-2019, the IMF reports the world's highest growth rate over 2022-24, averaging 47% a year. Crude oil made up 88% of its $20 bn goods exports in 2025, one of the most concentrated export baskets in the Americas, with gold (8%) the other notable export. Growth was 19.3% in 2025, FDI inflows equalled 33% of GDP, and GDP per capita reached $32,400, the highest of any South American country.

Haiti is the poorest economy in Latin America and the Caribbean, and its output shrank for a seventh straight year in fiscal 2025 amid gang violence, according to the World Bank; GDP fell 2.7% in 2025. Inflation reached 28.6% in 2025 and GDP per head was about $2,700. Net FDI inflows were negligible ($12 m in 2025), and no Comtrade goods trade has been reported in the last three years.
Heard Island and McDonald Islands, an Australian external territory, have no permanent residents; their surrounding waters host a catch-limited fishery for Patagonian toothfish and mackerel icefish.

The Holy See has no World Bank, IMF or Comtrade figures in the datasets. Its consolidated accounts show it is funded mainly by external donations and self-generated revenues, about half of them from real estate; in 2023 these made up 45% and 42% of income excluding its hospitals. It reported a small surplus of €1.6 m for 2024. It uses the euro.

Honduras is one of the poorer economies in the Americas, with GDP per capita of $3,600 in 2025, and depends heavily on remittances, which a Federal Reserve note puts above 20% of GDP in 2023. Coffee (18%) and insulated electrical wire (18%) led its $7.0 bn of goods exports in 2024, followed by palm oil and shrimp, and 47% went to the US. Goods imports were about twice exports, with refined fuel the largest item.

Hong Kong, a special administrative region of China, is a financial centre and, in the IMF's words, a "super-connector" between the Mainland and the rest of the world. Its goods trade is overwhelmingly re-exports, about 99% of exports in 2025 by official figures, so its $754 billion of goods exports in Comtrade far exceed its $427 billion GDP; integrated circuits (35%) and gold (11%) led, with 59% going to mainland China. FDI inflows reached $121 billion (28% of GDP) in 2025, and GDP per capita was about $57,000.

Hungary is a manufacturing hub for cars, electronics and batteries. Of its $166 bn of goods exports in 2025, cars led (7.8%), followed by computers, car parts and electric accumulators (3.7%), and Germany took a quarter. World Bank data show FDI net inflows of -$69.9 bn (-28% of GDP) in 2025, a large disinvestment on paper. The central bank, which says capital in transit distorts these data, reports that FDI in Hungary excluding it grew by €863 m in the fourth quarter of 2025. Growth was 0.5% in 2025 and government debt 74.6% of GDP.

Iceland's goods exports rest on fish and aluminium: Statistics Iceland reports that marine products made up 38.9% and aluminium products 34.5% of goods export value in 2025, and in Comtrade data unwrought aluminium alone was 31.0% of $7.2 bn of exports, with the Netherlands taking 34.4%. Imports include aluminium oxide (6.8%), a smelter input. Tourism is a major services export, directly generating a preliminary 8.8% of GDP in 2025. With 392,404 people, GDP per capita was $98,323 in 2025.

India is the world's most populous country (1.46 bn) and a $3.96 tn economy that grew 7.6% in 2025, though GDP per capita is only $2,700. It produced 27% of the world's rice in 2024 and led rice exports ($12.1 bn) in 2025, and it is the second-largest coal producer yet, narrowly ahead of China, the largest coal importer by value among reporting countries in 2025. Its $446 bn goods exports are diversified, led by refined fuel, smartphones and medicines, and services matter too: the RBI puts software services exports at $221 bn in 2025-26.

Indonesia dominates world nickel: it mined about 60% of global output in 2024 and holds 42% of reserves, and it is the second-largest cobalt producer. Its $282 billion of goods exports in 2025 were diversified across coal (9%), palm oil (9%), ferro-alloys (6%) and nickel intermediates, with China taking 24%. With 286 million people and a $1.45 trillion GDP, it is Southeast Asia's largest economy; it grew 5.1% in 2025, with government debt at 41% of GDP.

Iran combines large hydrocarbon resources with very high inflation, 42% in 2025, when GDP shrank 2.8%; the World Bank links the recent contraction to falling exports and limited access to foreign-exchange reserves as sanctions and conflict intensified. It was the third-largest natural gas producer (6.4% of world output) and fifth-largest crude producer in 2024, and oil and gas made up about 65% of its $104.5 bn goods exports in 2023, with China the top named partner (27%).

Iraq is heavily oil-dependent: crude oil was 90% of its $105 bn goods exports in 2024 (export concentration index 0.83), and IMF figures show oil providing over 90% of government revenue in 2024. It was the sixth-largest crude producer in 2024 (4.7% of world output). GDP shrank 2.2% in 2025, unemployment was 15.5%, and net FDI inflows were negative (-$7.6 bn), indicating disinvestment.

Ireland's headline figures are shaped by foreign multinationals: GDP grew 12.3% in 2025 and reached $131,592 per person, but the IMF treats modified gross national income (GNI*), which strips out multinational effects, as the appropriate measure of the economy. Goods exports of $291.3 bn in 2025 were dominated by pharmaceuticals (hormones 20.3%, blood and biological products 18.0%, medicines 11.3%), with 42.5% going to the USA. Net FDI inflows were $75.0 bn (10.4% of GDP).

The Isle of Man, a dependency of the United Kingdom with 84,118 people, had GDP of $7.6 bn and GDP per capita of $90,015 in 2023, when output fell 2.0%. Official national accounts show an economy built on services: in 2023/24 insurance was the largest sector (16.9% of the economy), followed by online gambling (eGaming, 14.2%), professional services (13.8%), other finance and business services (10.2%) and banking (8.6%). No recent Comtrade report is available.

Israel is a high-income economy ($60,300 GDP per capita in 2025) built on technology: the Israel Innovation Authority puts high-tech at about 58% of total goods and services exports in 2025, mostly software and other services. Its $58.7 bn goods exports in 2025 were diversified (concentration index 0.034), led by integrated circuits (8%) and diamonds (7%), with 11% unspecified, and the United States took 28%. FDI inflows were $26.2 bn, and government debt was 68% of GDP.

Italy is a $2.55 tn economy (2025) with a highly diversified export base: $727 bn of goods exports in 2025, led by medicines at just 7.6%, and a goods-and-services surplus of $49 bn. It is also a major commodity importer, ranking fifth among reporting countries for natural gas imports ($26 bn) and fourth for wheat in 2025. Government debt was high at 137% of GDP and growth was slow at 0.5% in 2025.

Tourism, remittances and alumina underpin Jamaica's external accounts; the IMF (2025) credited strong tourism revenues and high remittances for current-account surpluses in the two fiscal years to 2024/25. Alumina made up 34% of goods exports in 2025 and refined petroleum 25%, and the island holds 6.9% of world bauxite reserves (2024). GDP was $22.7 bn in 2025 and grew just 0.1%, while unemployment was low at 3.3% and government debt stood at 66% of GDP.

Japan's $4.4 trillion economy stands out for its government debt of about 205% of GDP in 2025. It is a large capital exporter, with outward FDI of $218 billion in 2025 against inflows of $46 billion. Cars are its biggest export (14% of $738 billion in goods exports in 2025), alongside chips and chip-making machinery, with the US (19%) and China (17%) the main markets. Fuel tops its imports: it ranked second among reporters for gas imports and third for coal.

Jersey, a dependency of the United Kingdom that uses the pound sterling, has no World Bank, IMF or Comtrade figures in this dataset. Statistics Jersey puts its 2024 GDP at £6.86 bn, with financial and insurance activities generating about 38% of gross value added, followed by real estate (11%) and public administration (10%). GDP fell 0.7% in real terms in 2024, driven by lower bank net interest income.

Jordan has a diversified, mid-sized export base: knitted garments (16%), jewellery, phosphates (6%), medicines (6%) and potash fertiliser (5%) led its $13.3 bn goods exports in 2024, with the United States the largest buyer (25%). Imports were twice exports. The economy carries high government debt (84% of GDP) and very high unemployment (16.5%) in 2025, with GDP per capita of $5,350.

Kazakhstan is Central Asia's largest economy ($306 bn GDP, 2025) and a commodity exporter: crude oil was 51% of its $79.2 bn goods exports in 2025, followed by uranium and other radioactive elements (5%) and copper. It was the ninth-largest copper producer and the 11th-largest wheat producer in 2024. Growth was 6.5% but inflation reached 11.4% in 2025, and net FDI inflows were negative (-$0.9 bn), indicating net disinvestment.

Kenya is East Africa's largest economy at $135.9 bn in 2025, and its goods exports are well diversified. Tea (16.8%), refined petroleum (10.0%), cut flowers (9.3%) and coffee were the largest items in 2025, and neighbouring Uganda was the top buyer (14.5%). Imports of $21.7 bn were two and a half times exports, and government debt was 71.3% of GDP.

Kiribati lives on the ocean: fees from foreign vessels fishing its waters are a major source of government revenue, equal to 38% of GDP in 2025 according to the IMF, though below the pre-COVID average of 62%. The economy is small ($349 m GDP, about $2,600 per head in 2025). Government debt is low at 8% of GDP, but inflation reached 6.5% in 2025.

Kosovo's economy leans on its diaspora: personal remittances equalled about 17.3% of GDP in 2025, and the IMF has noted that remittances and diaspora investment help finance a wide trade deficit. The goods-and-services deficit was $3.8 bn in 2025, nearly a third of GDP ($12.5 bn). Kosovo adopted the euro unilaterally. GDP per person was $7,899 in 2025 and government debt low at 17.5% of GDP. There is no recent Comtrade report.

Kuwait lives on oil: crude (49%), refined products (34%) and gas (5%) made up nearly 88% of its $69.7 bn goods exports in 2025, and it was the tenth-largest crude producer in 2024 (2.9% of world output). Government debt is low at 15% of GDP, and GDP per capita was $32,300 in 2025. Most exports are reported with unspecified partners.

Kyrgyzstan's economy grew 11.1% in 2025 and leans on gold and migrant earnings: gold and precious-metal ores made up about 42% of its $2.6 bn goods exports in 2025, while remittances equalled 22% of GDP in 2023. Imports ($12.0 bn, 40% from China) far exceed exports, leaving a trade deficit of $8.8 bn, about 39% of GDP.

Laos stands out for its debt: government debt was about 89% of GDP in 2025, and the IMF assesses the country as in debt distress, relying on continued debt-service deferrals amid talks with China. The IMF notes that long-term electricity export contracts and FDI support its external balances. Goods exports of $6.0 billion in 2023 were spread across gold, paper, copper ore, iron ore and potash, going mainly to China, Vietnam and Thailand. Growth was 4.5% and inflation 7.7% in 2025.

Latvia has a small, diversified export base in which forestry stands out: sawn wood (4.3%) and fuel wood (3.2%) were among the top goods exports in 2025, alongside phones, medicines and refined fuel, out of a $22.4 bn total. Its Baltic neighbours Lithuania (18.2%) and Estonia (11.3%) are the main markets. Income was $46,137 per head at PPP in 2025, growth was 2.1%, and the economy ran a $2.2 bn trade deficit.

Lebanon has been in a deep economic and financial crisis since 2019, which the World Bank in 2021 ranked among the most severe crisis episodes globally since the mid-19th century. GDP was $26.0 bn in 2024 after a 7.1% contraction that year, inflation was 14.6% in 2025, and government debt stood at 139% of GDP. Goods imports ($17.3 bn) were four times exports in 2024, and remittances equalled about 31% of GDP in 2023.

Lesotho's economy leans on South Africa. The IMF credits strong Southern African Customs Union receipts and water royalties from South Africa, along with spending restraint, for the government's FY2024/25 fiscal surplus. In 2024 diamonds (23.5%) and goods classed as waters (HS2201, 18.5%) led goods exports, followed by garments; South Africa took 58.5% of exports and supplied 78.9% of imports.

Liberia's small goods exports ($469 m in 2025) rest on iron ore (43.7%) and natural rubber (28.8%), with palm oil third (10.1%); imports were about six times larger at $2.9 bn. FDI inflows of $500 m equalled 9.5% of GDP. GDP was $5.2 bn in 2025, or $915 per person, with inflation of 8.3%.

Libya is one of the most oil-dependent economies: the World Bank estimates the oil and gas sector at about 60% of GDP and 97% of government revenue. Output swings with oil production; GDP grew 13.4% in 2025 to $48 bn, about $6,450 per person. The IMF puts government debt at 153.8% of GDP, and unemployment was 18.8% in 2025. Libya has filed no Comtrade report in the last three years.

Liechtenstein, with about 41,000 people, has one of the highest incomes per head recorded ($220,167 GDP per capita in 2024). The IMF describes an economy built on specialised, export-oriented manufacturing (over 40% of GDP) and a financial sector focused on private banking and wealth management (about 20%), in customs and currency union with Switzerland and with EEA market access; more than half of its workers commute from neighbouring countries. Public debt is nearly zero (0.5% of GDP in 2025), and no recent Comtrade report is available.

Lithuania's largest export is refined petroleum (9.8% of $41.6 bn of goods exports in 2025), while crude oil is its biggest import (10.5%); furniture (4.8%) is the next-largest export. Trade is regional, with Latvia, Poland and Germany the main partners. The economy grew 2.9% in 2025, attracted $3.1 bn of net FDI inflows (3.2% of GDP), and keeps government debt moderate at 39.5% of GDP; income reached $56,838 per head at PPP.

Luxembourg is a global financial centre: the IMF reports that its investment fund industry, the largest in Europe and second in the world after the US, held assets about 80 times GDP at end-2022, and the financial sector supplies about a quarter of value added. GDP per capita was $147,252 in 2025. Its cross-border finance shows in huge FDI swings: net outflows equal to 100% of GDP and net inflows of -$33.1 bn in 2025. Goods exports were a modest $16.7 bn, led by steel sections.

Macao, a special administrative region of China, lives on casino gaming and tourism: the IMF put gaming at about half of GDP in 2019 and mainland visitors at 71% of tourist arrivals. GDP per capita was about $76,000 in 2025, the government had no debt, and its surplus on goods and services trade was $23.7 billion. Its goods exports are tiny ($1.1 billion in 2025), mostly jewellery, phones and watches, 92% of them sent to Hong Kong.

Madagascar has a varied export basket. In 2025 nickel (17.7%) led its $2.5 bn of goods exports, ahead of cloves, garments, vanilla and titanium ore. It was also the world's second-largest natural graphite producer in 2024, with 5.6% of output. Yet income was only about $600 per person in 2025, and France and the US were the main buyers.

Malawi depends heavily on one crop: unmanufactured tobacco was 66.8% of its $914 m goods exports in 2025, and Belgium was the main destination. Imports were over four times larger at $4.1 bn. The economy is under strain, with inflation of 28.4%, government debt of 96.6% of GDP, growth of 1.9% and income of about $670 per person in 2025.

Malaysia's economy is anchored in electronics: integrated circuits made up 32% of its $462 billion of goods exports in 2025 and 20% of imports, with Singapore, the US and China the main markets. Refined petroleum, petroleum gases and palm oil add a commodity base, and it was the second-largest exporter of rare-earth products among reporters in 2025. GDP was $472 billion with growth of 5.2% in 2025, and government debt was about 71% of GDP.

The Maldives is a tourism economy: tourism was the largest sector, at 19.2% of GDP in 2024, per the national statistics bureau. Goods exports are tiny ($145 m in 2025) and almost entirely fish, against $3.6 bn of imports led by fuel. Government debt is very high at 129% of GDP (2025), while FDI equalled 11% of GDP and GDP per capita was $14,600.

Mali's exports are concentrated in gold, 73.1% of its $3.6 bn goods exports in 2024, with South Africa (56.2%) and Australia (11.6%) the main buyers; cotton (9.0%) and live animals follow. Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire together supplied about 43% of its imports, and refined fuel made up a third of the import bill. GDP was $30.1 bn in 2025 ($1,193 per person), with growth of 5.6%.

Malta is a small, fast-growing services economy: the IMF says growth averaged close to 7% a year over the past decade, led by tourism, online gaming and professional services. GDP per person reached $47,907 in 2025, with unemployment at 2.9%. Its FDI flows are outsized, with inflows equal to 52% of GDP and outflows 41% in 2025. The European Commission names aggressive tax planning risks as the key challenge in Malta's tax system. Goods exports ($3.9 bn) are led by integrated circuits (20%) and medicines (15%).

The Marshall Islands depends heavily on external grants, notably under its Compact of Free Association with the United States: an IMF report puts grant revenue at over 30% of GDP, against tax revenue of around 15%. The amended Compact provides $2.3 bn over 20 years in grants and trust-fund contributions. Growth in FY2024 came mainly from a rebound in fisheries. GDP was $308 m in 2025, with government debt below 9% of GDP; no recent Comtrade report is available.

Mauritania exports a mix of minerals and seafood: gold (36.5%) and iron ore (26.3%) led its $4.5 bn goods exports in 2025, followed by molluscs (11.8%), frozen fish (9.8%) and copper ore (4.9%), with China, Canada and Switzerland the main destinations. GDP was $11.7 bn in 2025 ($2,198 per person), FDI inflows equalled 5.4% of GDP and unemployment was 10.3%.

Mauritius has one of the highest incomes in this region, about $13,000 per person ($33,700 at PPP) in 2025. The IMF says growth of 3.2% that year was supported by services, including tourism and financial services. Goods exports were a modest $1.6 bn, led by canned fish (15.3%) and sugar (12.1%), against imports of $6.9 bn. Government debt was high at 86.8% of GDP.

Mexico is a manufacturing platform closely tied to the United States, which bought 82% of its $666 bn goods exports in 2025. Computers (13%), cars, trucks and auto parts lead exports, while imports, heavy in electronic parts and components, come mainly from the US (38%) and China (20%). It is a $1.8 tn economy of 132 m people, holds 5% of world copper reserves and was the largest reporter of maize imports in 2025. Growth slowed to 0.6% in 2025.

The Federated States of Micronesia relies on US Compact of Free Association payments, about $140 m a year, which with other donor transfers the US State Department calls the single biggest source of national income; fishing-rights sales are another. GDP was $502 m in 2025 ($4,400 per head), growth was 1.1%, and government debt was low at about 9% of GDP.

Moldova depends heavily on migrants' remittances, which research finds boost consumption and growth, though the high level of imports weakens their effect. In 2025 goods imports ($10.9 bn) were nearly three times exports ($3.8 bn). Exports combine wiring harnesses (13%) with farm goods such as sunflower seeds, wheat, rapeseed and wine, and Romania is the main partner for both exports (29%) and imports (23%). Inflation was 7.8% in 2025 and GDP per person $8,622.

Monaco, a euro-using city-state of about 38,000 people, recorded GDP per capita of $288,002 in 2024, after 8.5% growth that year. According to Monaco Statistics, scientific, technical and administrative services, financial and insurance activities and wholesale trade together generated almost half (49.1%) of its GDP in 2022. No recent Comtrade report is available.

Mongolia is a mining economy tied to China: in 2023 coal made up 58% of its $15.2 billion goods exports and copper ore 17%, and 91% of exports went to China. Its coal exports of $8.8 billion ranked fourth among reporting countries. GDP grew 6.8% in 2025, but inflation was 8.6%, and FDI inflows equalled about 11% of GDP. With 3.6 million people, GDP per capita was about $7,100.

The IMF describes Montenegro as a small, tourism-dependent economy, and the World Bank estimated tourism's direct and indirect contribution at about 31% of GDP in 2019. With unilateral euroization, the country has no independent monetary policy. Goods imports of $5.7 bn in 2025 were about eight times exports of $723 m, which were led by electricity (17%). Unemployment was 13.6% in 2025.

Montserrat, a UK territory, is still shaped by the Soufrière Hills volcano: two-thirds of the island remains a designated exclusion zone, according to the UK government (2023). The UK supports the territory's budget, with up to £30.3 m made available for 2023–24 under that year's aid settlement. Its tiny goods exports ($6 m in 2024) were almost all sand and gravel. The project's datasets hold no GDP figures for it.

Morocco has a diversified, Europe-oriented export base: insulated wire and cable (14.0%) and passenger cars (13.6%) led its $88.8 bn goods exports in 2025, alongside mineral fertilizers (17.4% across two headings). Spain and France took over 40% of exports. GDP was $182 bn in 2025, with growth of 4.6% and inflation of just 0.7%, though imports ($112 bn) exceeded exports and unemployment stood at 9.0%.

Mozambique stands out for foreign investment: FDI inflows of $5.8 bn equalled 25.8% of GDP in 2025, an exceptionally high share. Exports are energy- and mineral-based, led by natural gas (25.2%), coal (21.4%) and aluminium (17.2%), with India and South Africa the top buyers. The economy itself shrank 0.5% in 2025, and income was about $630 per person, with government debt at 90.3% of GDP.

Myanmar's economy remains weak: GDP fell 2.0% in 2025 and inflation was about 21%, after the World Bank found in 2023 that, following COVID-19 and the 2021 military coup, output was still around 10% below its 2019 level. Natural gas is its largest export (21% of $14.6 billion in 2025), followed by pulses, rice and copper, with China and Thailand the main buyers. It was the third-largest rare-earth producer in 2024, with 8% of world output; GDP per capita was about $1,500.

Namibia is the leading exporter of uranium ore among Comtrade reporters: uranium ($1.4 bn) made up 20.8% of its $6.5 bn goods exports in 2025, followed by gold (17.2%), diamonds (12.5%) and fish. FDI inflows were sizeable at 9.6% of GDP. But unemployment was 19.3%, and growth slowed to 1.7%.

Nauru, with about 12,000 people, earns most of its public revenue from hosting Australia's Regional Processing Centre for asylum seekers, which the IMF says provided almost two-thirds of government revenue in FY2025; the IMF lists fishing licence fees and residual phosphate processing as the other parts of its narrow revenue base. GDP was $176 m in 2025, and inflation was relatively high at 6.1%.

Nepal relies heavily on migrants' earnings: the World Bank reports that remittances exceeded a quarter of GDP in fiscal 2024, far surpassing FDI, which was only $44 m in 2025. GDP per capita was $1,540 in 2025, unemployment 10.5%, and the trade deficit $11.3 bn, about a quarter of GDP. No Comtrade report has been filed in the last three years.

The Netherlands is a European trade gateway: Statistics Netherlands reports that about half of its goods exports in 2024 were re-exports of goods made elsewhere. Goods exports reached $737.6 bn in 2025, led by refined petroleum (7.4%) and semiconductor-manufacturing machinery (4.0%), with Germany taking 22.2%, and the surplus on goods and services was $149.5 bn. GDP per capita was $73,684 and government debt a moderate 44.7% of GDP.

New Caledonia, a French territory, is built around nickel, producing 3% of world output in 2024. Real GDP fell 13.5% in 2024: according to the IEOM, the May 2024 riots, on top of setbacks in the nickel sector, caused all economic indicators to collapse that year. Unemployment stood at 11.2% in 2025; no recent Comtrade report is available.

New Zealand is a high-income ($49,600 per head in 2025), food-exporting economy: dairy dominates, with milk powder at 14% and butter at 8% of its $47 bn goods exports in 2025, followed by sheep meat, fruit and beef. China is the largest buyer (25%), ahead of Australia and the US. Growth was weak at 0.5% in 2025, with unemployment at 5.1% and government debt near 55% of GDP.

Nicaragua is among the most remittance-dependent economies in the world: the World Bank ranked it fifth among low- and middle-income countries, at about 27% of GDP in 2023. Gold was its top goods export in 2025 (23% of $8.7 bn), followed by coffee, T-shirts and insulated wire, with the US taking 46%. GDP per capita was about $3,200 in 2025, and FDI inflows were relatively high at 6.8% of GDP.

Niger's exports are dominated by crude oil, 89.0% of its $2.1 bn goods exports in 2025, going mainly to Italy and the Netherlands; it also ranked 2nd among reporters for uranium ore exports in 2023 ($204 m). GDP per capita was just $775 in 2025; growth was 7.0% while consumer prices fell 4.5%, and rice was the largest import (20.2%).

Nigeria, with 237.5 m people, is an oil and gas exporter: crude oil (55.7%), petroleum gases (18.2%) and refined products (10.1%) made up 84% of its $56.1 bn goods exports in 2025, while refined fuel was also its largest import (23.9%). GDP was $291 bn in 2025, only $1,224 per person, and inflation 23.0%. It was also the world's 4th-largest rare-earth producer in 2024.

Niue, linked to New Zealand and using its dollar, has lost population faster than almost anywhere: more than three-quarters of people born there live overseas, mainly in New Zealand. Tourism was estimated at 28% of GDP before COVID-19, and donor funding, including New Zealand budget support, provides more than a third of government revenue. The project's datasets hold no recent GDP or trade figures for it.

Norfolk Island is an Australian territory that uses the Australian dollar and lives mainly on tourism, which the local council estimates made up about 36% of economic activity in FY2023. The project's datasets hold no GDP or trade figures for it.

Few economic figures are available for North Korea: the datasets hold no GDP, inflation or Comtrade report, only a population of 26.6 million (2025) and negligible recorded FDI. Its foreign trade is almost entirely with China, which accounted for 96.7% of the total in 2022 according to South Korea's trade agency KOTRA, as reported by The Korea Times. It mined about 2% of the world's tungsten in 2024.

North Macedonia's goods exports are concentrated in a few manufacturing lines: catalysts and reaction initiators made up 20% of its $9.0 bn of exports in 2025 and wiring and cable another 10%, while platinum was the top import (10%). The World Bank reports that firms in its technological industrial development zones, which received most state tax incentives, accounted for one-third of exports in 2020. Germany took 36% of exports. GDP was $19.1 bn in 2025 and unemployment 12.3%.

The Northern Mariana Islands, a US commonwealth, has an economy shaped by tourism, with visitor arrivals returning in 2022, and by a boom-bust cycle in casino gambling over the past decade, according to US statistics. GDP was $1.1 bn in 2022, about $23,800 per head, after a 16.6% rebound that year. More recent GDP and goods trade data are not available.

Norway is a major energy exporter: natural gas (32.9%) and crude oil (24.7%) made up over half of its $170.9 bn of goods exports in 2025, and it ranked second among reporters for natural gas exports ($54.5 bn); the UK and Germany are its main markets. Government petroleum revenues go to the Government Pension Fund Global, worth about NOK 21,300 bn at end-2025, almost four times GDP. Fish is the next export (5.5%), and GDP per capita was $94,594.

Oman is a mid-sized Gulf hydrocarbon exporter: crude oil (36%), refined products (21%) and natural gas (9%) made up about two-thirds of its $60.5 bn goods exports in 2025. It attracted relatively large FDI ($6.7 bn, 6.2% of GDP, in 2025) and kept government debt at 35% of GDP. GDP per capita was $19,900, lower than in most neighbouring Gulf states.

Pakistan, with 255 million people and GDP per capita of $1,600 in 2025, is a textile and rice exporter: bed linen (14%), trousers and suits (10%) and rice (8%) led its $30.8 bn goods exports in 2025, making it the fourth-largest rice exporter. Imports ($65.2 bn, 31% from China) are more than double exports and led by fuels. Government debt was 73% of GDP, and the World Bank ranks it among the five largest remittance recipients in 2023 (about $27 bn).

Palau is a tourism economy: the IMF estimates that tourism-related activity accounts for close to 40% of GDP, one of the highest shares in the Pacific, and it also relies on external grants under its Compact with the US. GDP grew 6.3% in 2025 to $345 m, about $19,500 per head. Net FDI inflows were large for its size, at 16.6% of GDP in 2025, while government debt was 53% of GDP.

The Palestinian economy is small and tightly bound to Israel, which took 84% of its $1.5 bn goods exports and supplied 54% of its $8.3 bn imports in 2023, including electricity (9% of imports). The World Bank estimates that Gaza's GDP fell by 83% in 2024 during the war. GDP per capita was $3,170 and inflation 9.8% in 2025, and unemployment was 24% in 2022.

Panama is a dollarised services economy built around the Panama Canal, logistics and a large financial sector; the IMF links its rapid income convergence to the canal's expansion and the growth of services. Goods exports are small ($1.7 bn in 2025). The closure of the Cobre Panamá copper mine in late 2023, which the IMF said contributed about 5% of GDP, cut growth to 2.9% in 2024, though copper ore was still 20% of 2025 exports. Growth recovered to 4.4% in 2025.

Papua New Guinea is a resource exporter: liquefied natural gas made up 38% of its $13.8 bn goods exports in 2024, followed by a precious-metal heading (16%), copper ore (9%), crude oil and palm oil, sold mainly to Japan, Australia and China. GDP grew 5.6% in 2025 to $32.5 bn, but income per head was only about $3,000. Net FDI inflows were negative in 2025 (-$1.2 bn), meaning foreign investors withdrew capital.

Paraguay is a farm and energy exporter: soybeans (21%), beef (19% frozen and fresh combined) and electricity (11%) led its $11.1 bn goods exports in 2025, with Brazil and Argentina taking 61%. The IMF notes that Paraguay uses less than half of its share of power from the binational Itaipú hydroelectric dam and exports the remainder to Brazil. It was the sixth-largest soybean producer in 2024. Growth was strong at 6.6% in 2025, and government debt was moderate at 38% of GDP.

Peru is the world's third-largest copper producer (11% of global output in 2024) and holds the second-largest reserves. Copper ore (28%) and gold (17%) led its $74 bn goods exports in 2024, with China taking a third. The economy ran a $27 bn trade surplus in 2025, inflation was 1.5% and government debt a low 30% of GDP.

The Philippines relies heavily on services and remittances: the World Bank cites remittances from overseas Filipino workers and services such as business process outsourcing and tourism as key drivers, and it was the fourth-largest remittance recipient in 2022 ($38 billion). Its goods and services trade ran a $66.7 billion deficit in 2025, while integrated circuits were 34% of goods exports. It is the world's second-largest nickel miner (9% of output, 2024) and was the top rice importer among reporters in 2025.

The Pitcairn Islands, a British territory with a resident population of 41 in March 2017, rely almost entirely on UK budget support, which totalled £3.0 m in 2017–18. The project's datasets hold no GDP or trade figures for it.

Poland is a $1.04 tn economy (2025) with a very diversified export base: no product exceeded 4.9% of its $414 bn of goods exports. Car parts, computers, furniture and seats lead, and Germany takes 27%. Growth was 3.6% in 2025, unemployment was 3.0%, and the economy ran a goods-and-services surplus of $29.7 bn. Poland also holds about 3.5% of world copper reserves, ninth largest in 2024.

Portugal is a tourism-heavy EU economy: tourism directly generated 8.1% of gross value added in 2024, and travel brought in almost half of service exports (47.9%), according to the OECD. Its goods trade is diversified and centred on Spain, which took 26% of exports and supplied 33% of imports in 2025; cars lead its goods exports (5.8%). GDP was $347 bn ($32,082 per person) in 2025, and government debt was 89.7% of GDP.

Puerto Rico, a US territory, is a manufacturing economy built on pharmaceuticals: manufacturing made up 44% of GDP in 2024, and pharmaceuticals and medicines about 77% of its manufactured exports, according to the island's economic development department. GDP reached $129 bn in 2025 ($40,600 per head) but grew only 0.3%. Under the federal PROMESA law it has restructured most of its public debt, though negotiations and litigation over its power utility's debt were still ongoing in 2025, according to the GAO.

Qatar is the world's largest exporter of natural gas by value among Comtrade reporters ($56.9 bn in 2024), and gas made up 60% of its $95 bn goods exports, mostly shipped to Asia (China 20%, Korea 14%, India 12%). With 3.0 million people it is one of the richest economies, at $72,500 GDP per capita ($128,900 at PPP) in 2025, and reported unemployment of just 0.1%.

The Republic of the Congo has a very concentrated export basket: crude oil was 90.7% of its $7.4 bn goods exports in 2024, and China took 53.6% of the total. Government debt was about 100% of GDP in 2025, and unemployment was 19.9%.

Romania's exports centre on the car industry: cars and car parts made up 16% of its $109 bn of goods exports in 2025, and Germany took 20%. The economy runs a large external gap, with a goods-and-services deficit of $22.5 bn (about 5% of GDP) in 2025. Growth slowed to 0.7% in 2025 while inflation reached 7.2%. GDP was $429 bn, or $22,538 per person.

Russia is a resource superpower. In 2024 it was the second-largest producer of both crude oil (11.6% of world output) and natural gas (15.3%) and the top producer of palladium (40%). It ranked third for nickel, platinum, tungsten, cobalt and wheat. Beyond direct oil and gas taxes, research finds that government spending of that revenue generates further, indirect budget revenue. GDP was $2.56 tn in 2025, with inflation at 8.7% and government debt low at 16.6% of GDP. There has been no Comtrade report for three years.

Rwanda was one of the fastest-growing economies in the region, expanding 9.4% in 2025. Gold was its largest recorded export (23.4% of $2.2 bn), alongside coffee, tea and niobium-tantalum ores. In 2025 it was the top reporter of tungsten ore exports. The DR Congo (39.5%) and the UAE (25.7%) were the main destinations. Government debt reached 64.7% of GDP.

Saint Helena is a remote British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic with its own Saint Helena pound; no GDP or trade figures are available in the project's datasets. Researchers describe an economy formally underwritten by the UK government and supported by remittances from islanders abroad, with tourism seen as a key sector since the island's airport opened it up to visitors in 2017.

Saint Kitts and Nevis, with about 47,000 people and GDP per head of $25,200 in 2025, leans on citizenship-by-investment (CBI) revenue: a sharp fall in CBI receipts pushed the fiscal deficit to 11% of GDP in 2024, according to the IMF. ECCU members with CBI programmes collected government CBI revenue averaging 6.5% of GDP in 2019–23. Government debt was 59% of GDP in 2025; no Comtrade goods trade has been reported recently.

Saint Lucia's economy turns on tourism: after 4.7% growth in 2024, the IMF expected a slowdown in 2025 as temporary hotel closures and reduced airlift weighed on arrivals, and World Bank data show output fell 0.6% that year. Government debt stood at 77% of GDP and unemployment at 9.5% in 2025; the IMF flags high debt and large rollover needs as key vulnerabilities. No Comtrade goods trade has been reported in the last three years.

Saint Pierre and Miquelon is a small French overseas collectivity off Newfoundland that uses the euro; the project's datasets hold no macroeconomic or trade figures for it. The French overseas central bank IEDOM reports that fishing depends on resource availability and outlets, notably in Canada, and that landings fell in 2025 to their lowest level since 2013 amid scarce snow crab and the non-reopening of the Miquelon processing plant. Goods imports (about €100 m in 2025) dwarf exports (about €2 m).

Saint Vincent and the Grenadines carries government debt of 108% of GDP (2025, IMF WEO), after fiscal imbalances widened sharply following repeated external shocks, according to the IMF. Unemployment was high at 18% in 2025. The IMF has described tourism growth as a driver of its recovery; goods exports are small ($41 m in 2023), led by wheat flour (27%) and animal feed (17%) sold mainly to neighbouring islands.

Saint-Barthélemy, a French overseas collectivity that uses the euro, lives on high-end and luxury tourism: tourism made up 19.7% of GDP in 2023 according to France's overseas economic accounts (CEROM), and that demand feeds villa rentals, real estate and construction (13.8% of GDP). The French overseas central bank IEDOM describes accommodation and food services as the island's main employer. The project's datasets hold no GDP, population or trade figures for it.

Saint-Martin, the French part of an island shared with Sint Maarten, is a French overseas collectivity using the euro whose fragile recovery has been supported by tourism, according to the French overseas central bank IEDOM (2024). GDP was $649 m in 2021 ($21,700 per head), the latest available, and the population about 25,000 in 2025. No Comtrade goods trade is reported.

Samoa depends heavily on remittances from its diaspora, which the IMF says peaked at over 30% of GDP during the pandemic, alongside tourism. Goods exports were tiny in 2025 ($26 m, led by fuel and coconut oil) against $482 m of imports, mostly from New Zealand, Singapore and China. GDP grew 4.2% in 2025 to $1.3 bn, and government debt was 21% of GDP.

San Marino is a euro-using microstate of about 34,000 people, with GDP per person of about $59,900 in 2023. After the collapse of its offshore banking model around the global financial crisis, the IMF says, it diversified: the oversized banking sector shrank while manufacturing and non-financial service exports grew. With no physical border with Italy, goods, services and labour flow freely between the two. Government debt was 59.8% of GDP in 2025. There is no recent Comtrade report.

São Tomé and Príncipe is a micro-economy of about 240,000 people with GDP just under $1 bn in 2025. Its tiny goods exports ($31 m) were mostly cocoa beans (66.3%) and palm oil (14.6%), and the Netherlands bought 62.3%. Imports were nearly seven times larger, at $206 m. Inflation was 11.0%, and FDI inflows equalled 10.5% of GDP.

Saudi Arabia, a $1.28 tn economy, is the largest crude oil exporter among Comtrade reporters ($165 bn in 2025) and produced 11.2% of the world's crude in 2024, third globally. Crude and refined oil made up 66% of its $312 bn goods exports in 2025. Growth was 4.5%, government debt 32% of GDP, and FDI inflows $32.6 bn in 2025; China supplied 28% of imports.

Senegal's $10.0 bn goods exports in 2025 were led by crude oil (26.4%), gold (16.9%) and refined petroleum (14.6%), ahead of phosphoric acid and frozen fish, with neighbouring Mali the largest buyer (16.1%). The IMF puts government debt at a very high 127.7% of GDP in 2025, and FDI inflows were just $37 m. GDP grew 6.7% to $37.0 bn, about $1,955 per person.

Serbia is a diversified manufacturing exporter: no single product exceeded 6% of its $37.3 bn of goods exports in 2025. Copper stands out, with copper ore and refined copper together making up about 10% of exports, alongside wiring, tyres and car parts. Germany is the top export market (15%), while China is the largest source of imports (15%). GDP was $100 bn in 2025 ($15,262 per person), FDI inflows were $3.9 bn (3.9% of GDP) and government debt was 42% of GDP.

Seychelles is a small, high-income island economy of about 123,000 people, with income of roughly $19,400 per person in 2025. A 2017 IMF study found tourism contributes directly about a quarter of value added and is the main source of foreign currency, with tuna exports and fuel re-exports by the bunkering industry the other main earners. In 2025 canned and frozen fish made up about 59% of goods exports and refined fuel 30%.

Siachen Glacier is a large glacier in the East Karakoram; a satellite study found no significant change in its total area between 1980 and 2014. It is listed as a disputed area, and the project's datasets hold no population, macroeconomic or trade figures for it.

Sierra Leone is a mineral exporter: the IMF says the extractive sector provides about 80% of goods exports but only some 7% of GDP, drawing on reserves of rutile, bauxite, iron ore, gold and diamonds that are mostly exported with little processing. GDP was $7.5 bn in 2025, about $846 per person, with growth of 4.6% and inflation of 7.5%. Sierra Leone has filed no Comtrade report in the last three years.

Singapore is a rich trade and investment hub: GDP per capita was about $99,000 in 2025, and FDI inflows of $159 billion equalled 26% of GDP. Goods exports of $566 billion, close to GDP, were led by integrated circuits (24%) and refined petroleum (9%). Its gross government debt of 166% of GDP is unusual: the IMF notes it is issued mainly for non-spending purposes, such as investing pension (CPF) savings and developing the bond market, and that the government holds net financial assets.

Sint Maarten, part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, is a small tourism-dependent island whose tourism density is among the highest in the Caribbean, according to the IMF. Tourism and the completed reconstruction of its airport supported growth in 2025, according to the regional central bank; the World Bank puts growth at 3.4%, on GDP of $1.9 bn and $43,000 per head. No Comtrade goods trade has been reported in the last three years.

Slovakia led the world in car production per person for six years running to 2019, according to the U.S. International Trade Administration. Cars made up 28% of its $125 bn of goods exports in 2025, and car parts another 6%. Research finds the industry was built on foreign automakers' investment, leaving the economy heavily dependent on foreign capital. Germany and Czechia are the main markets. GDP per person was $28,544 in 2025, growth slowed to 0.8%, and government debt was 61.4% of GDP.

Slovenia's goods trade is dominated by pharmaceuticals: medicines made up 39% of its $80.8 bn of exports in 2025. Switzerland took 42% of exports and supplied 24% of imports, where heterocyclic organic compounds were the largest item (23.5%). As a result, its export concentration index (0.162 in 2025) is far higher than that of neighbours such as Croatia (0.012). GDP per person was $37,376 in 2025, and unemployment 3.2%.

The Solomon Islands is a small, low-income economy (GDP $1.7 bn, about $2,100 per head in 2025) whose exports remain dominated by logs sold to China, according to the UN, despite some decline in recent years. Government debt was moderate at 30% of GDP in 2025. No Comtrade report is available for recent years.

Somalia has filed no Comtrade report in the last three years, so its goods trade cannot be shown in detail. GDP was $13.0 bn in 2025, about $660 per person, and the goods and services trade deficit was $9.0 bn. The World Bank attributes the slowdown in growth to 3.0% in 2025 mainly to a sharp fall in foreign aid and poor weather, with robust remittance inflows cushioning households. Unemployment was 18.9%.

South Africa is the largest and most diversified economy in this region, with GDP of $427 bn in 2025.
