It is the world's leading platinum producer, mining 71% of global platinum and 37% of manganese in 2024. Its 2025 goods exports of $116 bn range from platinum (10.2%) and gold to cars and iron ore. Unemployment of 32.4% and net FDI disinvestment (-$2.2 bn) in 2025 stand out.

South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands is a British territory whose waters host a licensed toothfish fishery; the government says it invests about £1 m a year in fisheries management and scientific research. The project's datasets hold no economic figures for it.

South Korea is a $1.87 trillion manufacturing exporter built around semiconductors: integrated circuits made up 20% of its $709 billion goods exports in 2025, followed by cars (10%), refined petroleum and ships. China (18%) and the US (17%) are its main markets. It is also one of the largest raw-material importers, ranking second to fourth among reporters in 2025 for crude oil, gas, coal, iron ore and lithium. Growth slowed to 1.0% in 2025, with unemployment at 2.7%.

South Sudan is almost entirely an oil economy: crude made up 99.3% of its $3.3 bn goods exports in 2025. A rupture on the export pipeline through Sudan in February 2024 halted crude loadings and cut oil output, and inflation reached 91.4% that year. The IMF records 41.4% growth in 2025.

Spain is a $1.91 tn economy (2025) and a tourism heavyweight. Its travel surplus of $73.8 bn in 2024 was the largest in the OECD, and travel brought in 48% of its service exports, according to the OECD; tourism directly accounted for 6.0% of GDP in 2023. Goods exports ($433 bn in 2025) are diversified, led by cars (9.1%), with France (14%) and Germany (10%) the top markets. Unemployment remained high at 10.4% in 2025, and government debt was 100.5% of GDP.

Sri Lanka is recovering from a severe crisis: it suspended external debt service in April 2022, defaulted on its international sovereign bonds in May 2022, and entered a four-year, roughly $3 bn IMF programme in 2023. In 2025 growth was 5.0%, prices fell 4.8%, and government debt was 97% of GDP. Its $13.1 bn goods exports in 2025 are diversified, led by tea (11%) and apparel, with the United States the main market (23%).

Sudan's economy has been devastated by the armed conflict that began in April 2023: the World Bank estimates real GDP fell about 29% in 2023 and a further 14% in 2024, driven by destruction of infrastructure concentrated in Khartoum and the world's largest displacement crisis. For 2025 the IMF puts inflation at 99.9% and government debt at 204% of GDP. GDP was $60 bn in 2025, about $1,165 per person; Sudan has filed no Comtrade report in the last three years.

Suriname is a small, gold-dependent economy: gold made up 48% of its $3.4 bn goods exports in 2025, and almost all the rest is recorded as unspecified commodities, with 98% of exports going to unspecified areas. FDI inflows were exceptionally large at 45% of GDP in 2025, which the IMF links to investment in developing offshore oil fields. Government debt was high at 97% of GDP and inflation 9.2% in 2025.

Sweden is a diversified industrial exporter: cars (6.5%), medicines (4.0%), refined petroleum and blood products led its $208.5 bn of goods exports in 2025, with Germany, Norway, the USA and its Nordic neighbours the leading markets. Government debt is low at 34.5% of GDP, and inflation was just 0.7% in 2025, but unemployment was relatively high at 8.7%. GDP per capita was $63,133, and growth 1.5%.

Switzerland's goods trade is dominated by gold: unwrought gold made up 35.4% of its $553.5 bn of goods exports and 41.5% of imports in 2025, because, as the Swiss National Bank notes, refineries in the country produce about a third of the world's refined gold, and swings in gold flows reflect global demand rather than Swiss economic fundamentals. Beyond gold, pharmaceutical products dominate exports, with watches also in the top five, and the USA is the top market (21.9%). GDP per capita was $114,769 and inflation just 0.2% in 2025.

Syria's economy has been devastated by conflict: a World Bank estimate based on night-time light data suggests economic activity contracted by about 84% between 2010 and 2023. Official data are dated and sparse: the latest GDP figure is $23.7 bn for 2022, about $1,060 per person, the latest inflation figure is for 2019, and there has been no Comtrade trade report in the last three years. Population was 25.6 million in 2025.

Taiwan's economy is driven by electronics: its Ministry of Finance reports record goods exports of $641 billion in 2025, 74% of them information and communication products and electronic components, on demand for AI and cloud computing. IMF figures put GDP at $921 billion in 2025, with growth of 8.8% and GDP per capita of about $39,500 ($90,000 at PPP). Government debt is low at 24% of GDP. The datasets hold no UN Comtrade report for Taiwan.

Tajikistan is one of the world's most remittance-dependent economies: remittances equalled 39% of GDP in 2023, second only to Tonga, according to the World Bank. With GDP per capita of $1,640 in 2025 it is the poorest Central Asian state. Its small goods exports ($1.3 bn in 2023) mix cotton (16%), precious-metal ores (12%), aluminium (11%), antimony (9%) and electricity (8%).

Tanzania's exports are led by gold, which made up 47.2% of its $10.1 bn goods exports in 2025, and South Africa was the main destination (28.8%). Tobacco, edible nuts, coffee and copper ore follow far behind. The $90 bn economy grew 5.9% in 2025 with low inflation (3.3%), and Tanzania holds the world's fifth-largest natural graphite reserves (2024).

Thailand is a broadly diversified manufacturing exporter: its $340 billion of goods exports in 2025 were spread across computers (7%), phones (5%), gold, chips and trucks, with the US taking 21%. It is also a major food exporter, second among reporters for rice exports ($4.7 billion in 2025), and the IMF describes foreign tourist arrivals as a key growth driver. Growth was 2.4% in 2025 with slight deflation (-0.1%), and government debt was about 65% of GDP.

The Gambia earns much of its foreign exchange outside goods trade: remittances, which the central bank put at a record $776 m in 2024, now rival tourism as a source of foreign currency. Goods exports were only $50 m in 2024, led by groundnuts, against $988 m of imports. GDP was $2.6 bn in 2025 ($919 per person), government debt 73.7% of GDP and FDI inflows 10.6% of GDP.

Timor-Leste has lived on offshore oil and gas: production ceased in 2025, and the IMF reports an economy dependent on public spending financed by withdrawals from its Petroleum Fund, worth 939% of non-oil GDP in 2024 but at risk of depletion by the end of the 2030s. Crude oil was still 65% of its small $164 million of goods exports in 2023, with coffee at 9%. GDP per capita was about $1,340 in 2025, and the US dollar is its currency.

Togo has a relatively diversified export base: natural phosphates led with 17.4% of $1.7 bn goods exports in 2025, followed by plastic packaging, refined fuel, oil-cake and motorcycles; India was the top buyer (19.4%), followed by neighbours Côte d'Ivoire, Burkina Faso and Benin. The World Bank describes Togo as a regional logistics hub built around the Port of Lomé. GDP was $11.9 bn in 2025, with growth of 6.3% and inflation of 0.4%.

A 2011 study ranked Tonga, with Samoa, among the world's most remittance-dependent countries. Its recorded goods exports are very small ($29 m in 2025, against $312 m of imports): 79% fell under a single heading, HS4907 (unused stamps, banknotes and similar printed papers), and New Zealand took 87% of the total. GDP was $679 m in 2025, with inflation at 5.6%.

Trinidad and Tobago lives on oil, gas and petrochemicals: natural gas (23%), ammonia (17%) and acyclic alcohols (15%) led its $7.9 bn of goods exports in 2025, and the IMF (2026) ties its fiscal and external positions to energy prices, urging that energy windfalls rebuild the Heritage and Stabilization Fund. GDP fell 0.8% in 2025, government debt stood at 84% of GDP, and net FDI inflows were negative (−$794 m), meaning net disinvestment.

Tunisia's $20.0 bn goods exports (2024) are diversified and tied to Europe: insulated wire and cable led with 15.0%, followed by olive oil (7.8%), petroleum and garments, while France, Italy and Germany together took about 54% of exports. GDP was $57.5 bn in 2025 ($4,657 per person), with growth of 2.5%, unemployment of 15.1% and government debt of 81.7% of GDP.

Türkiye is a large ($1.60 tn GDP in 2025), highly diversified industrial economy: its $273 bn goods exports in 2025 had one of the lowest concentration scores (0.012), led by cars (5%) and refined fuel, with Germany, the UK and the US as top markets. Its most unusual feature is persistent high inflation, 34.9% in 2025, while government debt stayed low at 24% of GDP. It was also the tenth-largest wheat producer in 2024.

Turkmenistan is a state-led natural gas economy: the World Bank estimates gas at 68% of exports in 2023 and hydrocarbons at about 90%, with China taking 80% of its gas exports, and it holds the world's fourth-largest proven gas reserves. Government debt is just 3% of GDP (2025). It files no Comtrade report, so goods trade cannot be checked independently.

The Turks and Caicos Islands, a UK territory that uses the US dollar, are highly concentrated on tourism: S&P Global Ratings estimates that tourism indirectly accounts for about 65% of GDP and credits its resilience to sustained US demand, as reported by the territory's government in 2026. GDP grew 5.6% in 2024 to $1.7 bn, or $37,500 per head. No Comtrade goods trade has been reported in the last three years.

Tuvalu, with fewer than 10,000 people and GDP of $57 m in 2025, is one of the world's smallest economies. Its public finances rest on volatile fishing licence fees and grants: the IMF put licence fees at about 45% of GDP and grants at 28% in 2024. Public debt is very low at 2.8% of GDP (2025), and no recent Comtrade report is available.

Uganda's trade is dominated by gold, which was both its largest export (50.0% of $12.8 bn) and largest import (33.9% of $18.9 bn) in 2025. The UAE received 40.5% of exports. Coffee is the main home-grown export at 19.2%. The $62 bn economy grew 6.3% in 2025, with FDI inflows of $3.4 bn (5.4% of GDP).

Ukraine's wartime economy depends on large-scale external support. The IMF put its external financing gap at $136.5 bn for 2026–29, to be covered by the IMF, the EU, G7 economies and bilateral support. In 2025 its goods-and-services deficit was $56.8 bn, over a quarter of GDP, and government debt was 107% of GDP. Ukraine remains a farm-export powerhouse: sunflower oil, maize and wheat made up a third of its $41.7 bn goods exports in 2024, and it ranked fourth among reporting countries in both wheat and maize exports.

The UAE is both an oil power and a large trader: its $570 bn goods exports in 2023 included crude (29%) and refined oil (15%), making it the second-largest crude exporter among Comtrade reporters, alongside sizeable trade in gold and phones; gold was 9% of exports and 16% of imports. Half of exports were reported with unspecified partners. FDI inflows were $48.2 bn in 2025, and GDP per capita $50,300 in 2024.

The UK is a services-led economy: the House of Commons Library reports a £195 bn services trade surplus in 2025 that partly offset a £213 bn goods deficit (both excluding precious metals). Its goods trade figures are inflated by gold, which made up 14.4% of $554.9 bn of goods exports and 16.3% of imports in 2025; the Library notes that gold trade is volatile and does not add to GDP. Other leading exports are jet engines (9.6%) and cars. GDP was $4.00 tn in 2025 and government debt 102.1% of GDP.

The United States is the world's largest economy, with GDP of $30.8 tn and about $90,000 per person in 2025. It is the top producer of both crude oil (19% of world output) and natural gas (25%) in 2024 and grows 31% of the world's maize. It also runs a large external deficit: goods imports of $3.5 tn exceeded exports of $2.2 tn in 2025, with Mexico and Canada the largest partners. General government debt reached 124% of GDP in 2025.

The US Virgin Islands depend heavily on tourism, which became even more dominant after the 2012 closure of the HOVENSA oil refinery cost some 2,000 jobs; rebated federal excise taxes on rum are an important source of government revenue, according to the Congressional Research Service. GDP was $4.7 bn in 2022 ($44,300 per head), the latest available figure, and unemployment was 11.4% in 2025. No Comtrade goods trade is reported.

Uruguay has one of the highest incomes in South America, with GDP per capita of $25,200 in 2025. Its $11.3 bn goods exports are farm- and forest-based: frozen and fresh beef together about 24%, soybeans 14%, logs 9% and dairy 6%. Free zones are recorded as the largest destination (19%), ahead of China and Brazil. Government debt was 66% of GDP in 2025.

Uzbekistan, Central Asia's most populous country (37.1 million), grew 7.7% in 2025. Gold dominates its goods exports, at 38% of $19.7 bn in 2024, followed by cotton yarn (6%), and remittances equalled about 15% of GDP in 2023. Imports, led by China (29%) and Russia (22%), far exceed exports, with a trade deficit of $19.6 bn in 2025, about 13% of GDP.

Vanuatu is a small tourism-dependent economy (GDP $1.4 bn in 2025) that also earns unusually large public revenue from selling citizenship: the IMF puts citizenship-programme revenue at about 7% of GDP in 2024, down from 14% in 2020. The 2024 liquidation of the national airline and a December 2024 earthquake hit tourism and growth. Growth was 3.1% in 2025 and government debt 36% of GDP.

Venezuela's economy remains in deep distress. Oil is its major export, and an IMF study describes a decade-long fall in real GDP among the largest in modern history, driven partly by plummeting oil production, and one of the longest bouts of hyperinflation on record. Inflation was still 252% in 2025 (IMF), GDP per capita was about $3,500 and net FDI inflows were negative (-$522 m), meaning disinvestment. There is no recent Comtrade report, so export composition cannot be shown from the project's data.

Vietnam has become an electronics assembly hub on the back of foreign investment: smartphones (15%), display modules and chips led its $353 billion of goods exports in 2023, and research links its strong comparative advantage in electronics to a surge of inward FDI. The US took 28% of exports, while China and South Korea supplied half of imports, led by chips. GDP grew 8.0% in 2025, government debt was 31% of GDP, and it was the third-largest rice exporter among reporters in 2023.

Wallis and Futuna, a French territory using the CFP franc, has an economy centred on the public sector, which generated 55% of value created in 2019, up from 47% in 2005, according to the IEOM. The public sector is also the main employer and drove job growth in 2024. The project's datasets hold no recent GDP or trade figures for it.

Western Sahara is a disputed territory, largely under Moroccan control, where the Moroccan dirham circulates; no GDP or trade figures are available for it in the project's datasets. Its best-known resource is phosphate rock from the Bou Craa deposit, discovered in 1964 in the colonial era, and research on the territory's resources also covers fisheries and oil exploration.

Yemen is among the poorest economies in the region, with GDP of $7.9 bn and $418 per person in 2025, and inflation of 20%. The World Bank reports that conflict, a blockade on oil exports and falling aid kept the economy under severe strain in 2025. Its small goods exports ($602 m in 2024) went mostly to Saudi Arabia (58%) and include fish, while fuel, wheat and rice lead imports.

Zambia is a copper economy: unrefined copper anodes (51.8%) and refined copper (14.8%) made up two-thirds of its $11.3 bn goods exports in 2024. Switzerland (42.5%) and China (20.8%) were the main destinations. Government debt was about 100% of GDP in 2025 and inflation 13.9%.

Zimbabwe is a mineral and tobacco exporter. In 2024 gold (34.0%), tobacco (17.9%) and nickel products led $7.4 bn of goods exports, and it was the world's second-largest platinum and fourth-largest lithium producer. It has operated a multicurrency system in which the US dollar circulates alongside local currency. Inflation remained high at 81.4% in 2025, even as GDP grew 8.1%.
